source_metadata.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Czech mořiti, from Proto-Slavic *moriti, which is a causative to *merti (“to die”) (i.e. it means "to cause dying"). Compare mořit – Etymology 2, and also mor, smrt, mařit and můra.

examples.english: The justiciar ordered to put them into shackles, tortured them with hunger, and a soldier was commanded to slash their thighs with a club.
examples.ref: 1907, Jan Herben, Do třetího a čtvrtého pokolení, volume 1, Emil Šolc Knihkupectví, page 304:
examples.text: Justiciár dal je zakouti spolu do želez, mořil je týden hladem, a každý den voják měl poručení, aby je bil palicí po stehnech.
examples.translation: The justiciar ordered to put them into shackles, tortured them with hunger, and a soldier was commanded to slash their thighs with a club.

source_metadata.etymology_text: Related to Proto-Slavic *marati (“to dirty”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-/*mor- (“to blacken, to dirty; dirt spot”). Compare mourovatý.

examples.english: Aluminium can be pickled and polished if it has been dipped in strong solution of alcaline potash and then in petrol.
examples.ref: 2004, Šimon Vondruška with Miroslav Oehm and Jan Mohr, Zámečnictví: Tradice z pohledu dneška, Praha: Grada Publishing, →ISBN, page 57:
examples.text: Hliník možno mořit a leštit, vloží-li se nejprve do silného roztoku alkalické potaše a na to do benzinu.
examples.translation: Aluminium can be pickled and polished if it has been dipped in strong solution of alcaline potash and then in petrol.

unused_menu_senses.translation: to pickle (to treat a metal surface to remove impurities)

unused_menu_senses.translation: to stain (to coat a wooden surface with a stain)
